intro: Every match needs a start. In judo, players bow. In boxing, a bell rings. In school wrestling, two wrestlers shake hands and a whistle blows. In fencing, the referee calls out in French.
Matches also need rules. Rules say who meets whom. They say what gear to wear. In this unit, you will meet boxing gloves, fencing masks, weight classes and the groups that write rule books.
By the end, you can name how a room starts a match. You can tell one rule that keeps players safe. You can tell when girls and women got their own matches.
bigQuestion: How do signals and rules make a match fair and safe?

timeline.t: Jack Broughton writes boxing rules in London
The Queensberry Rules ask for gloves and three-minute rounds
Kano Jigoro opens the Kodokan judo school in Tokyo
The International Fencing Federation begins in Paris
The NFHS begins to write rules for high school sports
Women fence at the Olympics for the first time
Electric scoring comes to Olympic épée
Judo joins the Olympics in Tokyo, with weight classes
Women's judo joins the Olympics in Barcelona
The IHSA holds its first girls wrestling state final

write.prompt: Pick one sport from this unit. Tell or draw how a match starts. Then tell one rule that keeps players safe or fair. Name the rule book or group and the year.
tips: Use a word from the unit, like bow, bell or salute.
